Okay, so I think we can start. Thanks everyone for coming, I know it's late on a Thursday and half of you came straight from work, so I'll try to keep this to about twenty minutes and then we can just talk. The plan for tonight is pretty simple. I want to tell you how the community garden went this year, what worked, what really did not work, and then what we would like to try next spring. If you have questions in the middle, just shout, it's fine, I would rather answer them while the thing is fresh than collect them all at the end and forget half of them.

So, a bit of background for the people who are new. The garden sits on the old parking lot behind the library. The city gave us the lot three years ago on the condition that we take care of it ourselves, which mostly means we pay for the water and we keep the fence from falling over. The first year we had eleven beds and about fifteen people. This year we had thirty two beds and something like sixty people who came at least once, which is great, but it also means that a lot of the habits we had when we were small stopped working, and that is really the story of this year.

Let me start with the good news, because there is a lot of it. The tomatoes were ridiculous. I do not know what happened, maybe it was the compost, maybe it was the weather, but the south row produced so much that we ended up giving crates to the food bank every Saturday from the middle of July until the end of September. The food bank people told us it was the first time they had fresh vegetables that were not a donation from a supermarket that was about to throw them away. That made me really happy, honestly. The beans did well too, and the pumpkins, although the pumpkins mostly did well at taking over the paths, which we will get to later.

The second piece of good news is the school. The primary school down the street started bringing a class every Wednesday morning. The teacher, Maria, had this idea that every kid gets one square of soil, about the size of a pizza box, and they are responsible for it the whole season. Some of them planted radishes, some planted sunflowers, one boy planted a single potato and then checked on it every week like it was a pet. By the end of the year those kids knew more about watering than some of the adults, and I am including myself in that. They also made the signs you saw at the gate, the ones with the drawings of worms.

Now the less good part. The watering schedule completely fell apart in August. When we were fifteen people, we had a group chat and somebody would just say I am going tonight, and that was enough. With sixty people the chat became noise. People muted it. Some beds got watered three times in one evening and some beds did not get watered for a week, and during the heat wave we lost most of the lettuce and a good part of the herbs. Nobody did anything wrong exactly, it is just that nobody could see the whole picture. I think that is the main lesson. When a group grows, the thing that used to happen naturally needs somebody to actually own it.

The second problem was tools. We had one shed and one lock, and the key was hidden under a brick that everyone knew about, including, it turns out, people who are not in the garden. In June somebody took both wheelbarrows and the good hose. We replaced them, but it cost us most of the money we had set aside for new seeds. After that we got a combination lock, and that worked, mostly, except that the combination changed twice and the second time the message did not reach everybody, so for about ten days half the group could not open the shed at all.

The third problem, and this one is a bit sensitive, is that a few beds were basically abandoned. People signed up in March full of energy, planted something in April, and then we never saw them again. I understand, life happens, people move, people get busy. But an empty bed in the middle of the garden turns into a weed nursery very quickly, and then the weeds move into the neighboring beds, and then the neighbors are annoyed, and then we have a conflict that is really about dandelions but feels like it is about respect. We had two of those conversations this summer and neither of them was fun.

So what do we want to do differently? I have four proposals, and I want to be clear that these are proposals, not decisions. We will vote on them at the January meeting, and if you have better ideas I genuinely want to hear them.

The first proposal is a watering rota with names on it. Not a chat, a simple table on the shed door and the same table online, with two people assigned to each evening. If you cannot make your evening, you swap with somebody and you write the swap on the table. It sounds bureaucratic, I know, but the people I talked to who run bigger gardens all said some version of the same thing, which is that a written rota is boring and boring is exactly what you want for watering.

The second proposal is about the shed. We would like to buy a key box with a code that we can change from a phone, and only the coordinators can change it. It costs about ninety euros, which is not nothing, but it is a lot less than another wheelbarrow and another hose. We would also like to engrave the tools with the name of the garden, which apparently makes them much less attractive to steal, because nobody wants to explain why they have a shovel that says Library Lane Community Garden on it.

The third proposal is the hardest one, and it is about the beds. We would like to introduce a simple rule. If a bed has not been touched for four weeks during the growing season, a coordinator sends one friendly message. If there is still nothing two weeks after that, the bed goes back to the shared pool and somebody from the waiting list gets it. And yes, there is a waiting list now, there are nineteen people on it, which is a sentence I never thought I would say about a former parking lot.

The fourth proposal is more of a wish. I would like us to have a proper compost system. Right now the compost is three pallets tied together with wire and a lot of hope. It works, sort of, but it smells in summer and the neighbors have complained twice. There is a design that some other gardens use, with three bays that you rotate, and if a few people are willing to spend two Saturdays building it, the material costs maybe two hundred euros. We could apply for the small grant from the district for that, the deadline is in February, and I am happy to write the application if someone helps me with the photos and the budget.

Okay, let me talk about money for a minute, because people always ask. This year we spent a little over twelve hundred euros. Most of that was water, which was about five hundred, then seeds and seedlings, about three hundred, then the replacement tools after the theft, about two hundred and fifty, and the rest was small things like twine, gloves, the first aid kit and the coffee for the work days. We took in about nine hundred from the membership fees and three hundred from the plant sale in May, so we ended the year roughly even, with a tiny bit left over. If we do the key box and the compost, we will need either the grant or a slightly higher fee, and I would really prefer the grant, because the whole point of keeping the fee low is that anybody can join.

Speaking of the plant sale, that was honestly one of the best days of the year. We set up tables at the gate, people brought seedlings they had grown on their windowsills, the kids from the school sold lemonade, and somebody's uncle played the accordion for three hours without stopping. We sold almost everything. I would love to do it again, maybe twice, once in spring and once in autumn with bulbs and cuttings.

There are also a few small things I want to mention quickly. The rain barrels worked really well, and we should add two more on the north side of the shed. The bench by the gate needs new boards before somebody gets a splinter in a place they will not want to talk about. The bees are doing fine, according to Thomas, who looks after them, and he says we can expect a little honey next year if the winter is not too wet. And the bird that kept stealing the strawberries is still undefeated. We tried a net, we tried shiny tape, we tried a plastic owl. The bird does not care about the owl. I think the bird has made peace with the owl.

One more thing about volunteers. We are going to need two new coordinators, because Anna is moving to Hamburg in March and I would like to step back a little, not completely, but I have been doing this for three years and I think the garden is healthier if more than two people know how everything works. Being a coordinator means maybe two or three hours a week in the season and almost nothing in winter. You answer messages, you keep the rota up to date, you open the shed for deliveries, and once a month you sit in a meeting like this one and pretend you know what you are doing. If that sounds like you, come and find me afterwards, or send me a message, no pressure.

Okay, I think that is everything from my side. I talked for longer than I promised, sorry about that, I always do. Let us take a short break, there is tea and there are still some of those biscuits that somebody's grandmother made, and then we can go through the questions. And if you have to leave early, that is completely fine, the notes from tonight will go out by email on the weekend, together with the table for the watering rota so people can already start thinking about which evening they want. Thank you all, really. This was a good year, even with the lettuce.

Right, we are back. The first question was from Peter, who asked whether the watering rota means people lose their freedom to just come by whenever they want. No, not at all. You can come whenever you like, you can water your own bed every day if you want to. The rota only makes sure that on every single evening there are at least two people who are responsible for the shared beds and for checking the hoses are turned off. Think of it as a floor, not a ceiling.

The second question was about the waiting list and whether people on it can help before they get a bed. Yes, please, and thank you for asking. People on the waiting list are very welcome at the work days, and if they show up regularly, we would like to give them priority when a bed becomes free. That seems fair to me, but again, we can talk about it in January.

Somebody asked about pesticides, because a neighbor saw a spray bottle in the shed. That bottle is soap and water for the aphids on the roses, nothing else. Our rule since the first year is no chemical sprays and no artificial fertilizer, and I do not think anyone wants to change that. If you are not sure whether something is allowed, ask a coordinator before you use it, that is always the easiest way.

Lena asked whether we could grow more things that are easy for beginners, because the first months can be discouraging when everything you plant dies. That is a really good point. Next year we could make a small starter bed near the gate with plants that almost never fail, like zucchini, chard, nasturtiums, and mint in a pot so it does not escape. New members could start there with a buddy before they take over a whole bed of their own.

Then there was a question about the opening hours of the gate. At the moment the gate is open from seven in the morning until nine in the evening, and that will stay the same. In winter we will lock it earlier, at around six, because it gets dark and the path is uneven. If you need to come at a different time for a good reason, write to the coordinators and we will figure something out.

The last question was whether we could have a small celebration at the end of the season, something like a harvest dinner. I love that idea. We could cook together in the community kitchen at the church across the street, they already said we can use it once a month. Everybody brings one dish made from something that grew in the garden, and we eat at the long tables outside if the weather is kind to us. Let us aim for the second Saturday of October and see who wants to organize it.

I think that covers everything. Thanks again for staying so long, and see you all at the next work day.
